segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about the times and the seasons, brothers and sisters, you have no need for anything to be written to you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord comes just like a thief in the night.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When people are saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Peace and security,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then sudden destruction comes upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will certainly not escape.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness, so that the day should overtake you like a thief,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you are all children of light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to darkness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us stay awake and be sober.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk are drunk at night.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet the hope of salvation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not appoint us for wrath but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as you are in fact doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, to recognize those who labor among you and lead you in the Lord and admonish you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to esteem them most highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And we urge you, brothers and sisters: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both for one another and for everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice always,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: pray without ceasing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: give thanks in everything; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not quench the Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: do not treat prophecies with contempt,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but test everything; keep hold of what is good,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: keep away from every kind of evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may the God of peace himself make you holy through and through, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, pray for us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I put you under oath by the Lord that this letter be read to all the brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

notes.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine, but it was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members of a community. Since the letter is addressed to the whole assembly, “brothers and sisters” conveys what the first hearers understood. Several modern translations do the same; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

The phrase comes from Israel’s prophets, where it names the day when God intervenes to judge and to rescue. Paul applies it to the coming of the Lord Jesus described at the end of the previous chapter.

Many scholars hear in this an echo of Roman imperial propaganda, which advertised peace and security as the benefits of Roman rule. Others think Paul is echoing the prophets’ charge against those who cry “Peace” when there is no peace. The two are not exclusive, and the allusion is not certain.

notes.phrase: whether we are awake or asleep
notes.note: The verbs are the same ones used in verse 6 for moral alertness and moral slumber. Most interpreters take them here to mean being alive or dead when the Lord comes, picking up the concern of 4:13–18. A minority reads them as still meaning watchful or unwatchful.

The Greek verb can mean to preside over or lead, and also to care for or give aid to. Both senses were current, and translations divide between “are over you” or “have charge of you” and “care for you.” The three descriptions in this verse share one article in Greek and describe a single group of people.

notes.traditional: the idle (many modern versions); the unruly (KJV)
notes.note: The word describes someone out of line or undisciplined, originally of soldiers who break rank. Many modern versions have “idle” because the related words in 2 Thessalonians 3:6–11 are used of people who refuse to work, and papyri use them of shirking duties. The word itself is broader than laziness, so “disorderly” is used here.

notes.traditional: all appearance of evil (KJV); every form of evil
notes.note: The Greek noun can mean outward appearance or kind, sort. The KJV’s “appearance of evil” has been widely taken to mean avoiding whatever merely looks wrong, but most scholars and modern versions take the sense here to be “every kind” or “every form” of evil. The verb echoes the one in verse 21, a play the translation keeps with “keep hold of” and “keep away from.”

The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “make holy” keeps that link visible. Most traditional versions have “sanctify,” which means the same thing but now suggests a technical doctrine to many readers. The meaning is not disputed; the choice is one of clarity.

Some have read this as a formal statement that a human being has three parts. Most scholars take it as a piling up of terms for the whole person, in keeping with the stress on “through and through” and “whole” in the same sentence.
The Greek word means arrival or presence, and it was commonly used for the official visit of a ruler or high dignitary to a city. Paul uses it for the arrival of Jesus as Lord.

notes.phrase: I put you under oath by the Lord
notes.traditional: I charge you by the Lord
notes.note: The verb is strong: it binds the recipients by oath, with the Lord as the one sworn by. The letter shifts here from “we” to “I,” probably Paul speaking for himself. Letters were read aloud to the gathered community, and Paul insists that no one be left out.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
The verb ranges over urge, encourage, comfort and appeal across the New Testament, and the sense boundaries need fixing so the English does not vary arbitrarily.
It recurs in 1 Thessalonians, 2 Timothy and 1 Peter, and versions vary between “sober,” “self-controlled” and “clear-minded,” which obscures the drunkenness imagery.
It recurs in the Gospels, the letters and Revelation, where “watch,” “keep watch,” “stay awake” and “be alert” compete, and the link between passages is lost if the English varies.
It occurs in nearly every letter with senses ranging over favor, gift and thanks, and the split between “grace” and “favor” should be decided once.
